lesson.title: Finding the Line That Fits Best
lesson.summary: The least squares regression line is the unique line that minimizes the sum of squared residuals, giving the best linear summary of a scatterplot.
lesson.body:
Once a scatterplot shows a roughly linear pattern, the natural next step is to find the specific straight line that best represents it, not just to describe the trend qualitatively but to actually draw it and use it for prediction. Infinitely many lines could be sketched through a cloud of points, each looking reasonable to a different eye, so statisticians needed an objective rule for picking exactly one, and that rule is called least squares.

For any candidate line, each data point has a residual, the vertical gap between where the point actually sits and where that line predicts it should sit for the same x-value. The least squares line is defined as the one specific line that makes the sum of the squared residuals as small as it can possibly be, out of every line that could be drawn through the data, whether or not it looks appealing by eye.

Squaring is not an arbitrary choice. If the gaps were simply added up without squaring, positive gaps, points above the line, and negative gaps, points below the line, would cancel each other, and in fact for the least squares line itself those signed gaps sum to exactly zero regardless of how well the line actually fits, which would make a plain sum useless as a measure of fit. Squaring first turns every gap into a positive quantity before adding, so cancellation cannot hide a bad fit, and it also penalizes large misses much more heavily than small ones, which matches the intuition that one huge error is worse than several tiny ones spread across different points.

This minimization has a clean algebraic solution that reuses tools already built in earlier chapters. The slope of the least squares line, b1, equals r times the ratio of the standard deviation of y to the standard deviation of x. The intercept, b0, equals the mean of y minus b1 times the mean of x. Both formulas assume the relationship is genuinely linear in form, since fitting a straight line to a curved pattern, like the U-shaped example from the previous chapter, would badly misrepresent the data no matter how carefully the squares are minimized.

Returning to the five students, r was about 0.99, the standard deviation of hours studied was about 1.58, and the standard deviation of exam score was about 15.97. That gives a slope of about 0.99 times 15.97 divided by 1.58, which works out to 10.0. The intercept is then 69 minus 10.0 times 3, which is 39. The least squares line for this data is predicted score equals 39 plus 10 times hours studied, the exact line the next few chapters will draw, interpret, use for prediction, and check for fit using residuals.

This method is often called the line of best fit for exactly this reason, though best here has a precise, technical meaning: smallest total squared vertical distance, not smallest total distance measured some other way, and not simply the line that looks most centered to the eye. Other criteria are mathematically possible, minimizing the sum of the absolute values of the residuals instead of their squares, for instance, but squares are used because the resulting minimization is far more tractable algebraically, and because the resulting slope and intercept formulas connect directly back to the correlation coefficient and the standard deviations already calculated while describing the scatterplot.
